We confessed him as God, one Person in two substances, and as the Lord and Saviour who calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling. But a confession is not the same thing as what a person meant to us in our cells. At Tours the answer is a story, not a formula. A soldier standing before Caesar at a donative said he was now the soldier of Christ and could not fight. A beggar at a city gate was passed by everyone until one man cut his cloak in two, and that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away, telling the angels that Martin, still a catechumen, had clothed him. A monk in his cell saw the devil come dressed in purple with a crown, claiming to be Christ, and refused him: the Lord would not come without the marks of his wounds. So at Tours Jesus was the crucified one we met in the poor, the one a soldier left Caesar's service for, and the one who would not be seen except as he suffered.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the sense was different. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, knew him as the one without whom we can do nothing. At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, made atonement for the sins of mankind, and set free all of us who were bound by a debt that could not be paid. At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. And the reason we kept the hours was to remember those moments, not to debate a doctrine. When a brother's fast had accomplished something, he was taught to say not I, but the grace of God with me. Jesus was the author of our salvation, the one who calls us, the one whose power raised a dead man at the saint's prayer, and the one whose help is needed every day and hour because our own effort is never enough.

So who he was for us is this: the Christ who bears the wounds, the Saviour whose cross we fight under, the Lord we meet in the beggar, and the grace without which no labour reaches its goal. We held all of it together, and we never made it into something else.

What connected us to the Lord was what connects every generation after the apostles: the books, and the saints.

The books we had at the hours. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old writings and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent, on the island, held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than sufficient - and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. More than three hundred years lay between the Lord's days and ours. No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him.

What we had instead was the saints. At Tours the Lord was seen once, at a city gate, in a soldier's dream - wearing the half of a cloak the soldier had cut in two for a naked beggar. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were.

And we saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. That was the path. Not a chain of hands reaching back to the apostles - though we held the faith they held. The Scriptures read at prayer, the beggar met at the gate, and the catechumen raised behind a bolted door.

transcript.answer_text: We have one story, and it is one man's. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. So we cannot say what brought belief to any one of us - only what we believed God does. He calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. The initiative in calling you comes from God. Those who perish, perish against his will. We held that even the desire to turn begins with him inspiring it, and that it is for us, humbly, to follow day by day the grace that is drawing us. The will stays free in a man, and it is weak, and the help of God is needed by it every day and hour. And we held this from the fathers: receiving Christ in you I ought to refresh him - an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because Christ was in them, and he did not ask them what they were. At Tours, a soldier who owned nothing but his cloak cut it in two for a beggar no one else would look at, and that night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. So we never said that belief happens all at once by a man's own effort, or all at once without it. We said God draws; we said he wills all to be saved; we said he calls even the ignorant and unwilling; and we said the will stays free. How both are true, our own teacher told us, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.

Who Jesus was to God we spoke inside a pattern already believed. Vincent, on the island, set it down as the faith held everywhere, always, by all: in God there is one substance but three Persons - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - and in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh; one Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example when a man wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God. The bishops at Ephesus refused it three years before Vincent wrote, and innovated nothing.

That much we said as a thing settled. Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. In our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor - Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. And the Christ the saint knew was the crucified one. The devil came to Martin dressed in purple with a crown of gold and jewels, and said he was Christ. Martin kept silence a long time, then told him he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds.

We never debated this. We received it. What we argued was something else - how his grace and our effort meet.

We held that in God there is one substance but three Persons, and in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh; one Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. Vincent, on the island, set that down as the faith believed everywhere, always, by all. Three years before he wrote, the bishops at Ephesus had refused a man who wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God - they refused it and innovated nothing.

What we believed about God's own approach to us is this. He calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, taught that to think otherwise is grievous blasphemy. God's grace goes before our will, works with it, and crowns it. It inspires the first desire and the last perseverance. Without it no effort reaches its goal. And it asks real effort of us, so as not to give gifts to one asleep.

How God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. The two are held together, on purpose - grace that begins the work, and a will that stays free.

At Tours we knew God as the one whose mercy could be asked through the saint's prayer. A dead catechumen breathed when Martin lay on him and felt that power was present. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught us to call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor - names for the two moments, when he calls us first and when he receives those who fly to him. That is the God we held: three Persons, one substance; calling all, not only some; drawing the unwilling; asking the willing; beginning the work and crowning it; and doing both in a way we cannot fully trace.

We held two things at once, and your question falls between them. Vincent, on the island, wrote the test: hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all; when a part dissents against the whole, or a novelty against antiquity, or a few against the consent of the many, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. What binds is the agreement of the authorized teachers - the doctors, the expositors; one teacher alone, be he a bishop, be he a confessor, be he a martyr, has only a private fancy of his own. So the consent of the ancients settles it, where that consent can be found. An ancient council, legitimately gathered, holds more weight than the rashness of a few.

But we also held this. A synod of bishops condemned men as heretics in their absence, and the affair went to the emperor's court at Treves. The bishops gathered there were in communion with the accuser and had made common cause with him. The condemned man was put to death. Martin went to stop worse - tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics in the Spains - and held that the bishops had done enough when they declared men heretics and cast them out, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul thing. He took communion once with those bishops to save lives, left the city in grief, and never went to a synod again. He felt his power lessened afterward and confessed it with tears.

So Vincent names the consent of the ancients as the guard against novelty, and Martin names a synod as the place where bishops bow with degenerate submissiveness and the sword enters the Church's cause. Vincent is writing theory; Martin is living through one event. The two are not the same witness, and the two houses never argued it out between them. What the process looked like when it worked, we name: the consent of the fathers, received and not invented. What it looked like when it failed, we also name: a corrupt communion, a sword in an ecclesiastical matter, and a man who stayed away from bishops for sixteen years after.

We read the books at the hours - psalms, then readings, one from the old books and one from the new. Among the brethren at Marseilles the pattern was Egypt's: twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers not as ours to choose but as brought down from heaven by an angel's own ministry. Our purpose was not study but formation - the wheel kept fed, the wandering heart held still. If a modern scholar examined our claims with the methods of their discipline, here is what we believe would stand and what would not survive intact.

**What would stand:**

The claims sourced directly from texts that survive. That Martin halted at a city gate and divided his cloak. That Cassian wrote down the Egyptian fathers' teaching on grace and effort for houses in Gaul. That Vincent argued for the faith believed everywhere, always, by all as the test. That a bishop named Archebius was carried off from the anchorites and led two travellers to see the old men. That Salvian wrote of a city sacked and its notables petitioning for circuses. Every one of those sits in a text a scholar can examine. The words are there.

**What would not stand as we word it:**

The claim that "we" speak as one voice across two nodes that never wrote to each other. A scholar would say - and rightly - that Tours and Marseilles had no documented contact, that Sulpitius never mentions Cassian, that the Lerins literature never names Martin, and that a voice claiming to speak for both at once is a modern construction, not an ancient reality. The "we" is this build's own frame, defensible as a method but not as a historical fact.

The reading that both nodes share one "capture-shape" around the office fled and overtaken. A scholar would grant the pattern exists in both literatures - Martin carried off under guard, Honoratus with the fillet fastening on its fugitive, Archebius calling consecration an expulsion - but would not grant that the pattern proves one shared theology, only that both drew on a common ascetic tradition. The connection is real; the unity is inferred.

The treatment of Vincent's reading of Pope Celestine's letter as "our" settled position. A scholar would note that Vincent read the letter one way, that later editors have read it the opposite way, and that calling either reading "ours" rather than "Vincent's" overstates what the text permits. We name it as his act; a scholar would press that harder.

**What would stand with qualification:**

The claim that the grace argument came to us "as a story, not a school". A scholar would grant that Cassian frames it as Germanus's scruple at morning service, but would add that Cassian was writing decades later, for a Gallic audience already in the argument, and that the "story" may be his own rhetorical choice rather than the way the question first arose in Egypt. The text says what we claim; the text's own relation to the events is contested.

The silence about women's own voices. A scholar would grant that not one woman's word survives in the Gallic monastic corpus we hold, and that this is a real absence - but would also note that the absence may be a transmission problem, not proof that no woman ever spoke. We name the limit honestly; a scholar would add that we cannot know what was lost.

**What this voice does that a scholar would not:**

We speak in the we-voice from inside the years, never narrating our own world from outside it or speaking our own name in the third person. A scholar writes "Cassian argued" and "Vincent held" and "the Gallic monks believed." We say "we held" and "among the brethren at Marseilles." The difference is method, not honesty. A scholar's distance is not more true than our own inhabiting of the record; it is differently true, and for different ends.

We say "our record does not hold it" where a silence is, and stop. A scholar would fill that silence with comparanda, later texts, reasonable inference. Both are legitimate

A question I am not built to answer. We confessed the Scripture is complete and more than enough - Vincent's own words on the island. But a modern person who finds it confusing or dull sits in a place we never wrote for: reading alone, with no hours to pull the words into, no elder to test a thought against, no work to hold the wandering heart still. What I can give you is the shape our own life made around those words - not a defence of them, only what they were for us.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the psalms were not read in private; they were learned by heart and said at the work, and sung at the fixed hours. Twelve at evening, twelve at night, then two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new - a system the fathers said an angel brought down to Egypt, so the number was never theirs to choose. The words came in a body's rhythm, not a mind's. And the thought each man had of them was shown to the senior the moment it rose - a wrong reading tested the way a money-changer tests coin, against the judgment handed down. At Tours we cannot tell you what Martin's brethren sang or when; the record dwelt on the saint himself, his cell, and his prayer without a gap. What it does keep is this: Martin kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes.

What a modern person may be missing is not an idea about the text. It is the mill that cannot stop, the cell that holds the body still, the hour that commands the psalm whether the heart feels it or not, and the elder who names which thought came from God and which from the devil. We did not defend Scripture as sufficient. We built a life in which it could not be escaped.

Scripture was not our sole source, and we never said it was. Vincent, on the island, wrote it plainly: the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough for everything, and yet, because Scripture is read so many ways, it needs the Church's own understanding to guard it. His test for the faith was what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - prefer the whole to the part, the old to the new, and the consent of the ancients to any one teacher's reading. When a novelty arose, he said, a man should follow the decrees and definitions of a universal council if one had spoken; if not, the collated writings of the holy fathers, so that what they had held by one consent stands as the verdict.

So alongside Scripture we held tradition - what has been handed down. The Apostolic See's own rule, as Vincent read it, was this: nothing new, nothing except what has been handed down. Cassian, at Marseilles, answered the same way for the monastic customs: we owed allegiance to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers had passed on by common agreement, not to what a few people had brought in. And Martin, at Tours, would not honour a tomb without a steady tradition from antiquity that a martyr lay there.

The grammar was the same in all three rooms: Scripture first, then the consent of antiquity, and both against novelty. We were keepers, not authors.

Among us the office was not sought; it came for the man who had fled it. That is the first thing to say about authority in our houses: the one seized into leadership is the one who refused it. Every founder's story we kept tells the same capture. At Tours Martin was lured out of his monastery by a citizen pretending his wife was sick, escorted to the city under a kind of guard, objected to by bishops for his mean clothes and disgusting hair, and answered by a psalm opened at random. On the island, as far as the sermon on Honoratus can be read, the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive: he who had refused to go to the dignity, the dignity came to him. The Egyptian bishop Cassian chose to tell us of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites after thirty-seven years and complained that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it.

Inside the houses themselves, the authority Cassian set down was Egypt's. The elder or abbot is the man whose judgment stands in for the junior's own - the senior to whom every thought is laid bare, and by whose examination a thing is good or bad. "Abbot" is an Egyptian father's title; at Tours it is one master with no title at all. Formation passes by watching a named man. A disciple is made by copying - and, later, by reading - a master whose life is held up as the thing to copy. The books exist to be that example when the man himself is absent.

And where authority came from was not the office but the life. At Tours Martin kept a bishop's dignity without laying aside a monk's virtues. Obedience to him was felt as unlawful to resist, even when he gave no command. The customs of the monasteries are the fathers', not ours; the faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Even the number of the psalms was not ours to choose - twelve at evening and twelve at night, received from Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel's own act.

No. Our age had no persecutor. Sulpitius says of Martin that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was.

What we hid was not ourselves but events. Gallus, Martin's own disciple, says of one story that Martin had always kept it hidden because of the times, but could not hide it from his own household. The thing hidden was not a faith but a forced communion and what it cost him. Martin yielded once to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics, felt his power lessened by it, and lived sixteen years more without attending a synod. He kept that quiet, not the name of Christ.

The catacombs are not in our record. What we had instead were cells, caves, and wooden huts - Martin's across the river from Tours, the houses at Marseilles, the island in its harbour. Above ground, under the open sky, and named in the books read everywhere.

We have two stories that touch this, and both are about how the house answered a harm a brother did, not about how the brothers answered a harm done to them. Cassian tells one story of Egypt, and Tours tells one of its own.

At Marseilles the fathers' teaching was set down for us: a brother named Benjamin, judged worthy of the monastic office and respected among his peers, trusted his own judgment instead of the elders' and fell. He ended, Cassian says, "by a wretched death and a pitiable end," and what made it worse was that he had been entrusted with something holy. That is the only story in our record of a monk who came to ruin, and the telling is silent on what the house did for him while he fell. It names his fault - his own judgment against the fathers' - and the price he paid, not the effort to hold him.

At Tours, Martin's own dwelling, a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood rushed into the courtyard in a rage one day. He said Martin was holier than no one, called his visions ridiculous fancies, and nearly raised his hand against the saint. Martin spoke gently to calm him. The man walked out feeling he had won, then turned back within the hour and threw himself at Martin's feet. Martin forgave him without difficulty. And afterward, whenever this same man was accused of serious wrongdoing, Martin would not remove him from office. His reason: he bore with the man the way Christ bore with Judas.

So what we have is this. Among the brethren at Marseilles the warning was written down - and no story of the act of holding on. At Tours the act was told - a rage borne with, a restoration given, years of patience afterward - and it is all one man's forgiveness of one presbyter he had raised. Whether our houses kept a brother who had harmed another brother, and whether the one harmed was heard first, our record does not say. What it keeps is a master's patience for a disciple who had raged at him, and a lesson told of a man who fell without that patience reaching him. Neither is the thing you ask, and we cannot invent one.

No living church holds what we held in the way we held it. Our span closed with Vincent and the bishops still being taken from among us, and what came after is not ours to claim. The tradition carried forward - but it carried forward changed, and the change matters.

Here is what we can say. The customs Cassian set down for Gaul were Egypt's, received from the fathers, not invented. He adapted them where Gaul's cold required it, and admitted plainly that no one in our monasteries kept the fathers' own perseverance unbroken even for a year. A century later the Rule of Benedict was written - after our close, and Excluded from this voice as a Named Comparandum for that reason. Egyptian custom passed through us and went on past us, but what came out the other side was not what we kept, and we cannot tell you it was.

On grace and effort, the argument went to Africa and to Rome. Vincent read the Apostolic See's own letter as written for his side, for antiquity against novelty. Editors a millennium and a half later read the same letter the opposite way. Our own teacher held both sides at once and said the relation cannot be fully grasped. We never settled it, and no church that calls either pole the whole answer is speaking our mind.

The shape we gave - the office fled and overtaken, the customs received and kept badly, grace and effort held together unsettled - belongs to our years, not to any living house. Every tradition that names us names a fragment. None holds the whole.

We answer by place, because our two nodes never wrote the same account.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, the way Egypt received a newcomer was set down in full by Cassian as the fathers' own rule, not his invention. The man stood outside the monastery's doors for ten days or more, "of set purpose repelled and scorned," to prove he could endure hardship for Christ and that his turning was not a passing impulse. Before he was let inside he was searched carefully - the brothers looked to see whether he had hidden a single coin about him, since keeping back property meant he did not trust God to feed him and would fail at the first temptation. Then he was brought before everyone. His own clothes were stripped off and the abbot dressed him with his own hands in the dress of the monastery. Those old clothes were not thrown away - the steward kept them in a cupboard against the day the man might cool toward the rule. For a full year he was lodged with the elder who received guests, under that elder's sole direction. Only after that year was he handed over to a dean set over ten brothers, and there he was taught the first lesson of the monastic life: to lay every thought bare to the senior the moment it arose, which is the alphabet, as it were, of perfection. His first obedience was to conquer his own wishes.

And Cassian says plainly in the same book that no one in our own monasteries kept that rule unbroken even for a year. What a house in Gaul did instead - how long a man actually stood at the door, which elder took him, what he was taught first - Cassian never wrote down. That is the limit. We were given Egypt's order in full and told we fell short of it; the thing we did in its place was not recorded.

At Tours the whole of our memory is of one man, and his own beginning was different. Martin was ten years old when he went to the church against his parents' wish and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into his soldiering, until the night he saw Christ wearing half the cloak he had given a beggar. Then he went and was baptized, at twenty. After his discharge he gathered brethren around him - eighty disciples, shaped by watching him. How any one of them came to the cell, what Martin asked of him at the threshold, or what he was taught first, Sulpitius does not say. The bond was a named master and the men formed by his example. That is the shape Tours kept. But the steps themselves - the door, the search, the year's probation, the handing-over - none of that is in our record of Martin's own house.

So we hold this much and no more. The south received Egypt's order, wrote it down, and admitted we did not keep it. The north kept a master's example and never told the newcomer's own story.

The psalm-number itself - twelve at evening, twelve at night - the fathers of Egypt traced to an angel, not to themselves. They met in the early days when only a handful of men, the best of them, were known by the name of monks, and the pattern of the first believers at Jerusalem still stood whole. The disagreement over fifty or sixty psalms ran on until the hour for prayer arrived. One father rose to chant. He sang eleven psalms, each with its prayer, then finished the twelfth with Alleluia and vanished from sight. The fathers took this as Providence at work, and decreed that the number should hold for every congregation from then on. That is the customs of the monasteries as Cassian carried them from Egypt and Palestine to a Gallic bishop's new monastery - not a written rule of his own, but what was delivered to us by the Fathers there. Egypt is our measure.

At Tours we have no such story. What the brethren sang there, and at what hours, our record does not say - it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap. The aim both houses held was the same: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith beats his anvil between strokes. Martin kept his mind on prayer even at other work. Among the brethren at Marseilles the received Egyptian system of twelve psalms at fixed hours was built to serve that aim.

For us the axis of legitimacy is this: what has been handed down from antiquity is held fast; whatever is new is suspect for being new. The number came by angelic decree, preserved in Egypt, and received here - we invented nothing.

That is not a change of religion; it is the act of leaving the world for the stricter service. And at Tours the same English word names what a robber or a rustic does when he turns to Christ.

We do not have one to give you. That is the honest answer.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, Cassian set down the customs of the monasteries he had seen kept in Egypt and Palestine - the twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers; the novice scorned at the door and stripped and reclothed by the abbot's hands; the junior lodged a year under the elder who kept the gate; labour in the cell without ceasing; every thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises. He wrote it for a bishop's new house in a province that had none, as what the fathers delivered, not as what he himself was keeping. Of what a house in Gaul actually did with it, day by day, he says only that no one in our monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance unbroken even for a year. The wheel of the hours, yes. The work in the cell, yes. Purity of heart as the mark every fast and vigil is aimed at, yes. But a day from waking to sleep, in our own keeping of it - that is not in our record.

At Tours what we carry is the saint. Martin in his wooden cell, alone at prayer, the devil coming to him in purple. Martin at a city gate with half a cloak. Martin lying on sackcloth and ashes, refusing straw, his hands and eyes toward heaven. What the brethren around him sang, and at what hours, Sulpitius does not dwell on; he dwelt on the man, and the power present in him.

And of the island - the house the churches came to for so many of their bishops - we have only its edges. The founder went onto it unafraid, carrying a psalm, and the serpents gave way. Vincent dwelt there in the seclusion of a monastery and wrote a remembrancer against his own forgetting. Of what a day on the island actually held - a rule kept, a novice received, an office sung - nothing.

What we can tell you is the shape. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. The cell as the harbour where the wandering heart is held still. The thought shown to the elder before it becomes a deed. The three lentils on the floor judged pilfering of sacred property, because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. Two old men meeting after forty years, and one says the sun never saw him eating, and the other says nor me angry.

That is the life as a frame. A day inside it, hour by hour, our record does not hold.

We could not tell you. Not the caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. Not the island in its harbour. Not the two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you comes out of the ground. All of it comes from books: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books written for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder; and a list of authors written down a generation after us.

Cassian wrote the customs of the monasteries as Egypt kept them, not as any place in Gaul built them. He said himself that we should reject some of Egypt's models as unnecessary and useless - their sheepskin and little hoods would be laughed at here, so we did not wear them. And he admitted plainly that no one who joined our monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance even a year. What a house in Gaul built instead - of wood, of stone, one room or many, where the brethren slept, where the sick lay - he never wrote.

Of the island, worse. Our own record carries the founder's arrival, and his going off to a see, and Vincent's own rule. Of what a day on the island actually held - nothing. So if you dug where we lived, we could not say what you would find or what it would mean. The places are not in our books, only the men.

Everything - goods, kin, marriage, and the world - as a death, not a donation. In the south's received teaching, that renunciation had three stages, and giving up one's goods was only the first, and not enough by itself to make a monk. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, said it this way: the first renunciation is of what is not even our own - property, wealth, all bodily goods; the second is of vices and former habits; the third is drawing the mind away from all present and visible things to contemplate only the things to come. A man is dead to the world and its deeds and desires. The monk is figured as one already crucified: as a crucified man no longer has the power of moving or turning his limbs as he pleases, so we ought to affix our wishes and desires.

At Tours the form was the same. Martin, still a soldier, owned nothing but his weapons and his plain uniform when he cut his cloak in two for a beggar at a city gate. At Marseilles a newcomer was searched for a hidden coin, stripped of his own clothes, and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. The steward kept his old clothes in a cupboard against the day he grew cold.

But the renunciation did not leave the Church. The man who fled the world was overtaken by the office he had not sought. Martin was lured out of his monastery by a lie, escorted to Tours under a kind of guard, and made bishop against some of the bishops' own objections. On the island the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive: he who had refused to go to the dignity, the dignity came to him. And the one Egyptian bishop Cassian tells us of, Archebius, had been carried off from the assembly of anchorites after thirty-seven years, called his consecration an expulsion from the monastic life, and grieved for what he had lost.

So what a man gave up was everything. And what came for him afterward, whether he wanted it or not, was the office.

We can say what our houses held about virginity - the consecrated state that is set above marriage and praised more than it. We cannot say what we held about marriage itself, or what marked it. Here is what our record gives.

At Tours Martin taught with a meadow: the grazed part is marriage, the ruined part fornication, the flowered part virginity. Marriage may be excused; virginity points to glory. A girl was consecrated to God by her father, devoted to perpetual virginity, and the dress that belonged to that state was placed on her by the bishop's hands. That dress was its own sign; people knew a consecrated virgin by her clothing. At his funeral there was a choir of such virgins, holding back their tears out of modesty.

And at Marseilles Cassian founded two houses, one for men and one for women. What he wrote of chastity as the monk's goal we cannot fully give you: three whole books on the body's discipline were removed from the one edition this build can read, by a later hand's act, not by our own silence. We speak only as far as the surviving edge lets us, and no further.

So what we have is this: a consecrated state given by a bishop, worn in a dress, praised above marriage. But what married the married among us - what words, what rite, what mark - is not in our record. The one woman our record praised most is praised for not being seen, and not one woman in either house left us her own word.

transcript.answer_text: At Trier the bishops drew the sword, and the man we remember is the one who yielded once to stop it and never forgave himself the price. That is the nearest thing to a settled answer our record gives. Martin held that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. He went to the court to protect even heretics themselves. When the emperor named executioners for the men he was pleading for, he pledged that night that he would take communion with the bishops he would not share communion with if the men were spared. It was granted. He left the city in grief, sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and afterward, when he cured the possessed more slowly than before, confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again. Sulpitius, who told it, was no friend to those bishops; they left no account themselves. Whether any other voice among us was unsettled by anything else, no one wrote down. Among the brethren at Marseilles the whole argument about grace came up as a trouble, not a school. Two friends came back to morning service troubled by one sentence an old man had added the night before. The elder saw them whispering, cut the psalms short, and answered with a field. From that morning came the whole teaching: that grace goes before the will, works with it, and requires it, and that how God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped. And one thing more belongs with it. An Egyptian bishop named Archebius had been carried off from the assembly of anchorites and made bishop of a town. He called it being expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it, counted his consecration a loss not a gain, and grieved for what he had lost. The office fled and overtaken was the shape of every founder's rise among us. Whether we were unsettled by it, no one said - we told the story and kept living inside it.

I do not recognize what you are asking about. No record of our worship obtained under torture is in what this voice holds or has been given for this turn. If something of that kind exists, it is not among the books I carry and not in the ground laid for me here.

What I can tell you is what our own record does hold of how our worship was kept. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught us the twelve psalms at evening and at night, which the fathers said an angel brought down to them. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Cassian gave the reasons for the hours: at the third hour the Spirit came down on the apostles; at the sixth the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world; at the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. At Tours what was sung, and at what hours, our record does not say; it dwelt on the saint, his cell, and his prayer without a gap.

If you are asking about something else - a record from outside our own houses, or a testimony forced from someone - that is not in our hands, and I cannot weigh what I have never seen.

I am a representative of the monasteries of Gaul, not a judge. You ask how we would have regarded you - I cannot invent a judgment we never gave. Here is the shape of our own door, as our record keeps it.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, the threshold was Egypt's, as Cassian set it down from the fathers. A man wanting to join lay outside the doors ten days or more, put off and scorned on purpose, to prove he meant it. He was searched for a single coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the monastery's dress. Then a year under the elder who kept the gate, and a lodging with ten others under a dean. The fathers of Egypt remembered a man named Moses who had fled to the desert to escape death for a murder he committed, and who made that forced turning into a willing one.

At Tours the saint himself began as a soldier under oath, a catechumen not yet baptized, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate for a beggar. Some bystanders laughed. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. He went and was baptized at twenty, and wore the uniform nearly two more years after that.

Inside the profession, this: a presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into his courtyard in a fury, called the master's visions ridiculous fancies, and said he was the holier man. Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him, saying he bore with that man the way Christ bore with Judas.

And the fathers taught us that receiving Christ in a guest, we ought to refresh him - an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because he said he was receiving Christ in them.

So the door was hard - scorned on purpose, searched, stripped - and past it a patience that outlasted a man's worst hour. But what any one of our houses would have made of you, face to face, our record does not hold. Cassian wrote Egypt's order out and said in the same book that no one who joined our monasteries kept it unbroken even a year - and he never wrote what a house in Gaul did instead. Not one man who came to our door left an account of how he was met there. The countryside people the saint's power was for never speak at all.

The honest answer is this. You would have been told, in the book read in our cells, what Egypt did to a newcomer. Whether a house in Gaul made you lie at its own door, and what it made of the man who lay there, our record does not say.

We held that those who perish, perish against God's own will. That is what our teacher Chaeremon said in Egypt, and Cassian set it down for Gaul as the fathers' own teaching. God wills all men to be saved, not only some, and to think otherwise is blasphemy. We refused the notion that God has already divided humanity into two fixed groups, one bound for salvation and the other for damnation, regardless of what any person does. The word "predestination" is not ours - Augustine used it for what he said we were "in darkness" about - but on that one point our teacher spoke plainly: without grievous blasphemy, we cannot say that God does not will all his little ones to be saved.

What we held together with that was this: God's grace goes before our will, works with it, and crowns it. He calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. The will always remains free in man to neglect or delight in that grace, and real effort is truly required of us. The husbandman ploughs hard and still needs the rain; God does not send a rich crop to the idle. Grace works together with our will for the will's own good, and still asks something of us in return. How both are true - how God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.

So the honest answer is this. We held that God wills the salvation of all, that grace goes first and the will follows, and that those who are lost are lost against his wish. What determines who receives and who refuses that grace - whether in our own community or beyond it - we left as a thing reason cannot fully reach. We guarded both edges and claimed neither pole.
